title: End-State-Controlled Quantum Transport in Armchair Graphene Nanoribbon Artificial Quantum Materials
abstract: Artificial quantum materials based on atomically precise graphene nanostructures provide an ideal platform for exploring quantum phenomena arising from localized electronic states. Here, we develop a real-space theoretical framework to elucidate the microscopic origin of interface states in graphene architectures composed of $n$-triangulenes and armchair graphene nanoribbons (AGNRs). By continuously tuning the coupling between graphene building blocks, we reveal the evolution of triangulene zero-energy modes and AGNR end states into compact localized node orbitals at three-arm junctions. The number and chirality of these node orbitals obey a universal relation, $N_{node,δ}=|N_{es,t,A(B)}-N_{tri,0,B(A)}|$, where $N_{es,t}$ denotes the total number of AGNR end states contributed by the three AGNR arms at the junction, and $N_{tri,0}$ is the number of zero-energy modes of the attached triangulene. The chirality of the node orbitals is determined by the dominant constituent: when $N_{es,t}>N_{tri,0}$, they inherit the sublattice chirality of the AGNR end states ($δ=A(B)$), whereas for $N_{tri,0}>N_{es,t}$ they inherit that of the triangulene zero-energy modes ($δ=B(A)$). This real-space picture provides a transparent understanding of compact localized state (CLS) formation beyond conventional bulk topological descriptions. Using experimentally synthesized triangulene nanographenes as representative examples, we further explain the emergence of their zero-energy modes and quantitatively reproduce their tunneling spectra within an extended Anderson model. Finally, we demonstrate that these node orbitals can serve as elementary building blocks for constructing artificial graphene nanoribbons with highly tunable flat subbands near the Fermi energy. The resulting CLSs exhibit controllable degeneracy and strongly anisotropic quantum transport.
summary: This work develops a real-space theoretical model to understand interface states in graphene nanostructures formed by connecting triangulenes and AGNRs. It derives a universal rule linking the number of localized node orbitals to the end states and zero-energy modes of the constituent parts. This framework proves that these junctions can be engineered to create artificial nanoribbons with highly controllable flat subbands for quantum transport applications.
main_problem: The study aims to elucidate the microscopic origin of interface states in complex graphene architectures, moving beyond purely bulk topological descriptions.
main_result: The research establishes a universal relation governing the number and chirality of localized node orbitals formed at junctions, demonstrating that these sites act as elementary building blocks for constructing nanoribbons with tunable flat subbands.
method: A real-space theoretical framework using a tight-binding Hamiltonian is developed to model electronic structure evolution by tuning inter-building block couplings.
model_or_system: The system involves artificial quantum materials based on graphene, specifically Y-junctions formed by connecting $n$-triangulenes and armchair graphene nanoribbons (AGNRs). The analysis uses a single-$p_z$ orbital tight-binding model.
key_observables: Number and chirality of node orbitals ($	ext{N}_{	ext{node},\delta}$), flat subbands near the Fermi energy, and tunneling spectra.
important_parameters: The coupling strength between graphene building blocks ($t_{es}$) is a key tuning parameter; an applied longitudinal electric field (Stark effect) is used as a diagnostic tool.
main_assumptions: The primary assumption is that the interface states can be understood by analyzing the hybridization of end states and zero-energy modes, providing a real-space picture over bulk topological invariants.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate the structural components (triangulenes, AGNRs) and device configurations used for calculating electronic properties and transport spectra.
paper_structure: The paper first introduces the physical system and theoretical framework, then analyzes specific junction geometries (e.g., 3T-GNR/7y-AGNR/3T-GNR), derives the universal relation for node orbitals, and concludes by demonstrating their utility in designing tunable quantum transport elements.
why_interesting: The focus on localized, geometrically determined states (CLS) provides a concrete, real-space mechanism for engineering electronic properties in low-dimensional carbon systems, which is highly relevant for solid-state quantum devices.
